It's only now starting to get boring.
Now imagine this game, but with workshop levels.

I dont understand why this game has negative reviews about the gameplay. Dont get me wrong, there are valid criticisms like how there arent really keybinding options and stuff however half of them are complaining about how the game is dull and all you do is powerwash. This game is literally called powerwash simulator, what did you expect?

Step 1: Turn off the lights and brew up some hot cocoa.
Step 2: Put on your favorite music or something chill and calming.
Step 3: Boot up this game and let your mind wander.
Step 4: Reflect on life/perhaps get a little sad.
Step 5: Wash away the dirt and wash away the past.
Step 6: Feel better and clean.

This game is absolutely ridiculous. Swiping surfaces up and down in repetitive motions for hours. Cleaning a million nooks and crannies, sitting in front of the computer screen like a hypnotized zombie.
Two reasons why I recommend this game: One, it is the perfect game for switching off your brain, when you want to advance time and you don't have a cryosleep chamber nearby. Two, at some point playing this game, you will pause and be forced to consider whether or not you are living your life to the fullest. Hence, the repercussions of playing this game could lead to a dramatic existential crisis, when you realize all the precious heartbeats you have wasted while being zombified will never come back.

I got this game to help deal with my anxiety. For hours I would meticulously clean every career mode level with my elderly cat by my side, insisting on hindering me as much as possible by using my mouse hand as a pillow. When I got to the fishing boat I ended up having to say the last goodbye to her. Today I finished career mode and felt like a complete idiot choking up at the post credits scene. 20/10, would wash again. RIP Bathory, the best little black cat, 2008-2024.

If I had to describe the game in one word, it would be “therapeutic” because it’s a way to turn off your brain and focus on something basic.

I had to put my cat down last week and this game really helped me cope with losing my best friend. I didn’t wanna lay in bed all day but also didn’t wanna play anything that was intense in any way. I also have donkey brains so depression was super ramped up. This game actually helps me a lot with that.

If any devs ever come across this review, I just wanna say thank you for making this game because it really helped me out during a tough time. Also, this game is a lot cheaper than a trip to the nitwit doctor.

This game is amazing. I think a lot of people might think it's a dumb gimmick, like, "why would you want to WORK for fun?". First of all, this is a video game, it's nothing like real life powerwashing, so that's a pointless argument to have. It is an important question to ask, still. Why is this fun?

Simple, relaxing gameplay. No way to lose. Obvious and immediate progress / reward. A lot of different levels, funny easter eggs, themed DLC, co-op. It's not a very expensive game. Some days you get home from work and you just want to turn your brain off and chill for an hour. This is the perfect game for that, it's like a digital zen garden. It's really not that deep.

It's kind of hard for me to play this for more than an hour straight anyway since the bright colors and rote movements cause everything to blend together, causing a mild headache of sorts. But that's not the fault of the game, if anything that's a benefit so you don't waste too much time playing this game.

It's simple, it's stupid, it's fun, get it on sale.

Edit: Finally beat the main campaign and most of the bonus levels. 40 hours! Pretty hefty value for $25

I have played over 400 hours of this game and I will continue to do so.
I have just finished the main story line and all the maps are beautiful and just hella satisfying to clean. The game is relaxing and, as a person who routinely suffers from anxiety, I find the game almost like my ''happy place''. When I am having a bad day or anxious about a situation that has come up, this game helps.
I hope the developers know how much I love this game and I am hoping they will continue to update with new maps, even if the career mode is now complete. I would very much love to see new map updates, as this is going to be a game I will always return to. 
Thank you so much Power Wash Devs, it has been an awesome year of cleaning and I look forward to the years to come.

EDIT: Almost 2100 hours I've logged in this game. It sucks that I have to say this: do not buy any of the DLC except for nostalgia purposes. Be careful even then. That being said, not even my extreme Final Fantasy VII nostalgia could make me like the Midgar pack. Spongebob and Tomb Raider? Don't waste your money. This team has gotten away, FAR away, from the winning formula that made this game great. It was unique, it was innovative, but now it's banking on other brands for a fresh breath of life. Now, everything is an intense slog to find every tiny nook and cranny and getting just the precise angle to clean 99.9999% of every dirt speck because your completion thresholds are ridiculous. The base game is worth it, but don't bother with anything else.

Go back to what you started with. Expand on that. FINISH THE STORY. Stop trying to turn a buck because you rode the wave of popularity and are now too lazy to want to do anything but make bank off other people's creations, with or without their permission. 

Probably won't be playing this much more except when my friends want to play. This game has become a serious disappointment. 

EDIT: Almost 1600 hours in, and I am convinced I was a power washer in a previous life. 

I have no life now. I've sold all my worldly possessions except my PC and gaming setup. I live off ramen and multivitamins. I've reset my progress more than a speedrunner playing Ninja Gaiden. I see orange flashes in my dreams, and then I wake up only to be reminded that I missed three tiny specks on the last level I played, so I have to reset everything and start over. If God exists, when I meet them I will ask them one question: "can I get the extra long extension prior to the fire helicopter?" To which they will answer "no, my son, you gotta put in the work."

I picked it up at the beginning of this year when I was going through chemotherapy for breast cancer, as I wanted something I didn't have to think too hard about, and could do pretty mindlessly. I was more than surprised, though, by how much I genuinely enjoyed playing the game. The text messages from your clients and friends were funny, the overarching story was actually interesting, and the maps are fantastically well done. But the best part is that you don't even have to pay attention to any of that. You can just wash things. You're a passive participant in the storyline.

The actual wash mechanics are the best I've seen out of any simulator-type game. It is immensely satisfying. But all the other reviews are correct-- it is also immensely addicting.

My only complaint is that the second one hasn't come out yet. I've already purchased all the DLC and unfortunately can't re-purchase, but my wallet is ready and waiting for PWS2. I have definitely purchased it for some friends that wanted to help me clean things. Might go on a spree and get it for all my friends who have it on their wishlist... hmm.

This game comes with a really stupid simple premise that's done extraordinarily well - you spray water at things until they're clean.  Doesn't sound like fun, but it's incredibly soothing and satisfying to see something covered in mud and dirt suddenly pop with live and vibrant colors - and sorting out a method of which you tackle these projects is a different sort of fun in itself.  

Think of it like a coloring book from your childhood - except the giant building is the book and the pressure washer is your crayon.  The level of organization (or chaos) is up to you.  Do you want to spray a bunch of wangs in the mud?  Or do you just want to climb on top of the truck and start spraying from there?  The grime is your oyster.

Also, the game has a story for some reason.  The people you get the projects from text you while you clean their crap and it's hilarious and charming - there's actually a few of the reoccurring customers that I came to enjoy and looked forward to seeing if I get to do more for them!

Edit: No, seriously, this game has a story.  I'm not crying, I just got soap in my eye...

This game stands on a mighty pedestal above everything else with a half-ironic "simulator" title released in the past two decades. 

PowerWash Simulator is not a sim, and it knows that. Every object you clean is just a texture layered on another texture, and different nozzles/guns remove that texture more efficiently than others. You're waving a Photoshop delete tool around for twenty hours. 

The beauty of PWS comes from the writing. This isn't one of the dozens of shovelware Polish 'sim' games pumped out every quarter. The writing isn't edgy for the sake of being edgy to give streamers something to react to during the first two hours. Story and charming character work doesn't magically stop happening after the two hour Steam refund window is up. If anything, the breadcrumbs of story in PWS snowball into a big, goofy, overarching story about wacky occurrences in this small metro area that all - coincidentally - require the services of a professional power washer. 

If you've read this far, please take it from me: power through the tree house level. Keep in mind that hitting the C button to detatch your cursor and allow you to move the washer around the screen is a CRUCIAL tool. Ignore the stats on the washers, they're all direct upgrades.

This game is great for when you need to sit back and let your ADHD brain experience something soothing and something you can completely sink into. Similar feeling to using a real power washer or watching a video of one. I am a completionist myself and I speed through games like nobody's business; however, for some maps it takes me days to complete. It makes me want to take a break and come back to it the next day and most games can't hold my attention like that. Once again def get this game.

Please, give this game a shot. It's just amazing.

At first glance, PowerWash Simulator looks like a humble little “spray dirt, watch number go up” situation. You think: Oh, this will be relaxing. A background game. Something to pass the time.
Wrong. This game grabs you by the hose and whispers, “You will not stop until it’s 100%.”

The dopamine? Immaculate.
The satisfaction of watching filth melt away under a perfectly aimed stream of water? Transcendent.
The moment when ONE TINY SPECK is hiding somewhere on a roof beam and you rotate the camera like a feral raccoon trying to find it? Spiritual trial.

And then—AND THEN—
there’s the alien story.

Excuse me???
Why is my silly little pressure washer game suddenly dropping quirky, mysterious, slightly unhinged lore about aliens and strange happenings like it’s casually seasoning the experience with X-Files energy?? I did not expect to be emotionally invested while power-washing a town that may or may not be involved in extraterrestrial nonsense.

But I was.
Hooked.
Fully onboard.

This game is perfect for passing time, losing time, and accidentally entering a meditative state where nothing exists except dirt, water, and your unrelenting desire for cleanliness. It’s cozy. It’s funny. It’s weird. It’s way better than it has any right to be.

I loved it.
I will defend it.
And if you don’t understand the joy of seeing “Job Complete – 100% Clean,” then I am sorry, but you simply have not lived.

10/10, would wash again. 💦🛸

All the peaceful satisfaction of power washing, none of the soggy shoes.

I never expected to find PowerWash Simulator—a game about spraying virtual dirt off of fences, playgrounds, and ancient statues—to become my absolute favorite game of all time. But here we are.

What begins as a humble power washing gig in the fictional town of Muckingham slowly evolves into something almost spiritual. The gameplay loop is incredibly simple: point, spray, clean. But there’s a meditative rhythm to it, a kind of digital zen garden that sucks you in and doesn’t let go. Whether you're removing decades of gunk from a rusty fire truck or unveiling the clean lines of a dinosaur-themed playground, each job feels like a quiet triumph.

There’s no rush, no time limits unless you want them. No enemies, no fail state—just you, your washer, and the satisfying hiss of high-pressure water cutting through grime. It’s the ultimate escape. I’ve played late into the night more times than I care to admit, chasing that final 1% of invisible dirt on the underside of a ladder or the wheels of a monster truck.

It’s therapeutic. It’s oddly beautiful. It’s… perfect.

But I wouldn’t be honest if I didn’t mention what happened to my great uncle Bruce. A man of intensity and curious taste, Uncle Bruce took an interest in the game one afternoon after I told him it was “like pressure washing your soul.” He played for three straight hours, hunched in front of the monitor, completely locked in. Somewhere between cleaning the skate park and finishing the gnome-infested temple, he had a seizure.

Now, Bruce is fine. He’s fully recovered and insists that it wasn’t the game—it was “the intensity of the cleansing,” as he dramatically puts it. But it’s now part of our family lore: “The PowerWash Incident.” Every time I boot up the game, I think of Bruce, bless him, and his overly ambitious attempt to 100% the Ancient Statue map in one sitting.

So yes, my favorite game of all time nearly hospitalized a family member. But that’s just part of its legend now.

PowerWash Simulator is a masterpiece of calm, of slow-burn satisfaction, and of strangely compelling gameplay that proves you don’t need explosions or combat to feel accomplished. It’s not just a game—it’s therapy with a hose.

Uncle Bruce, this one’s for you.

As has been stated before: You don't need to read this. The game is solidly made. Anything beyond that is irrelevant, excepting one small detail I'll get into later, which can be easily ignored or attended based on your desires. You either saw Power Wash Simulator and said "Wait, really? That sounds incredibly dumb", and, for you, you were right, or you said "Wait, really? That sounds... Oddly satisfying", and, again, for you, you were right. You have already determined whether or not you will enjoy this game. You already know that answer. If you think you will enjoy the satisfying experience of stripping grime, spraypaint, rust, and more off of all kinds of nasty, gunk-caked architecture and vehicles, you are completely right, it will be amazing and you'll spend days with your eyes glued to the screen (watch out for eye strain!). If you think there's nothing particularly satisfying about this experience and you'd be better off playing literally anything else, you are completely right, it will be a waste of your time and not worth opening. Ask yourself which and go with your gut.

That said, my actual review of this game, from the perspective of someone who said "Wait, really? That sounds... Oddly satisfying".

I love this game. It's solidly made- the controls are simple, easy to grasp, not nearly perfect but I'm not sure you could make a perfect control scheme to replicate the actual use of a power washer outside of VR, and I don't have and am not fond of VR. There's different nozzles for different purposes, though I'm always stuck in the cult of the yellow myself. There's an ever-growing number of simple maps, frustrating maps, buildings, vehicles, big stuff, small stuff... They add a few every few weeks/months. There's no unreachable bits. Some cleaning-based games will accidentally have some tiny bits spawn outside the map or something like that and be uncleanable- that's not a problem I've had here. The few glitches that are present are being constantly fixed, like the endgame gif that used to show flashes of when you activate your magic dirt sense that highlights dirt, but now never shows the flashes, allowing you to enjoy the time-lapse of you clearing out all that nastiness.

The only issues I've had are the following:

On some very large objects, if you're cleaning too thoroughly, large patches can spontaneously disappear as you cross the game's threshold for cleanliness and the details are auto-cleaned for you. They're constantly working to refine this one to make the tolerances better and improve the game, but it's a tricky thing to manage.

There is "lore" in this game, which some people might get annoyed by. But it's minor and can be ignored pretty easily, especially once everything is unlocked so you can just do free play mode. New updates bring new lore.

Some of the items that need to be cleaned require awkward angles to clean them properly. There is never anything that cannot be cleaned, but it can get a little awkward. This is manageable, and it can even be kinda fun trying to figure out how the hell you'll get to the right spot to clean something.

Aside from those three, small issues... The game is fantastic. I get sucked in for hours on end, and I can't help but enjoy taking the high-end power washer back to the early maps, like the basic van, and cleaning it in seconds when it took me so long the first time. Great game, very enjoyable, very satisfying.

There's something about sitting down and just cleaning various objects that are incredibly dirty. It's like watching the "oddly satisfying videos" online, this has similar effect where it makes you feel good somewhere inside seeing the dirt go away. As such, it's rather catchy and addicting.
I've seen people stream this and was always a bit at the edge of my seat seeing how they approach the cleaning process and wanted to take control myself, then I spent the whole day playing this game after I got it, when I thought this would be a few hours endeavour, I practically have to stop myself from playing anymore whenever I launch this. It's super relaxing, there's no music playing, it's just ambient sounds and the sound of the water gun/water effects. You can easily put on some music/stream/show/whatever or comepletely zone out and focus only on the game and you leave feeling kind of refreshed.

Graphically this looks better than I'd expect from a game like this, tho the dirt "pixelation" can be seen on the edges when you slash your beam of watter through it, it's nothing that would be off-putting. There are no real physics in play either, your water jet kind of just "deletes" the dirt, it doesn't flow anywhere, neither does the water from your area of effect like you might expect in real life when watter flows on a surface, leaving traces behind itself, doesn't happen here, tho again, not an obstacle of any kind. Beyond that that water effects are really nice to look at.

Customization and tool upgrades are a nice goal to work towards, there are 4 washers in total, you start with one and can buy the other three with earned money. Each is just better than the previous one, there will not be an instance where you'd be thinking about which washer to use. I found that skipping the second one and buying the third one first is a viable option, and the upgrade feels great too. What you will be swapping are the heads of the washer, those will affect your beam of water, the wider it gets, the less pressure it's going to have, so while you do cover a bigger area, some dirt might stick anyway. Some surfaces are easier to clean so you can put on a wider one, where others you might need the narrowest one to clean a surface completely. Pressure also decreases the further away you are from your target.

Some cleaning jobs can be a bit frustrating, with many hidden corners to cover before you finally hear that satisfying "ding" when a part is finally fully clean. You never need to clean 100% of the area yourself, there's some leniency, without it, the game could get quite frustrating, so sometimes you still see some dirt on something you're currently cleaning but you claned enough surface area for the game to go *ding* and the rest of the dirt just disappears, there is a good balance with this, sadly for those who would rather not have this enabled, there's no option to get ridd of this. Maybe somewhere down the line the devs will include a mode where you absolutely do need to clean all the dirt yourself or you're out of luck. 
When you do manage to overlook some small part(s) on a big object, say a building, it can get really tricky finding the spots that still need cleaning, no arrow will guide you, you can only press a button that will make unclean surfaces bright orange for a moment so you may find yourself running around spamming that button, looking everywhere. At least you have an in-game guide where all the different parts are written out so you have a bit of an idea where to look but "window frame 9/10" is sometimes not quite enough. 
Walking on anything that isn't a flat surface isn't the smoothest experience either, movement gets jagged, it's not a huge issue, just a bit annoying. Thankfully you don't have to scale tilted rooftops very often and for most high-up jobs you get tools to work with like a stepping stool, ladder and in some cases even scaffolding.

Overall my experience with this game is very positive. It's a relaxing experience that I frankly can't get enough of. Considering this is early access, there is a lot of content to go through already, I am nearing 20 hours in and I have not seen more than half of the eareas that are in the steam screenshots, making me really excited to play more. This is very much worth your time if you're looking for something to chill with.

Unironically one of the best games I've ever played. I probably have actually thousands of hours in this game not tracked by steam. 

I cannot explain how satisfying and how much it scratches the deepest corners of my autism brain to systematically clean a giant boat for the 200th time from bow to stern.

Truly, I can never put into words why this game is so amazing. Admittedly, neurodivergence definitely plays a part. If I want to watch a really good video essay, but don't have the ability to sit still and listen, Power Wash Simulator on one screen is low commitment enough to help me absorb the information without interrupting me with intense mechanics.

Plus it's just super enjoyable on its own.

PLUS IT'S $25! And the DLC is well priced (most of the DLC is FREE and their roadmap basically says 60% of all DLC will continue to be).

It's hard to really encapsulate how playing the game feels. It's somehow both therapeutic and meditative at the same time. The mechanics are so simple, you just wash stuff. From musty old cars to grimy homes to disgusting fairground rides.

One only has to look at my whopping 130+ hours to see how engrossing it is. You get lost in the work, listening to the sounds of the water. On the other hand, there's no music whatsoever and this is probably an understandable design choice. We all feel motivated by different things and so allowing us to listen to whatever, including the silence, is something I'm okay with. In fact, the first few wash jobs I don't think I listened to anything beyond the spraying water.

The core game goes on a surprisingly long time with all sorts of neat things to scrub clean with your "angry jets of water." On top of that there's a number of side jobs that unlock as you progress through the main game, as well as several free DLC job packs for other Square-Enix (the publishers) property; Tomb Raider with Lara Croft's mansion and grounds, and stuff related to Final Fantasy VII. The Tomb Raider one was incredibly nostalgic for me, taking me back to when I played the old games back in the day.

There's also a number of paid DLC packs that I [i]haven't[/i] purchased so your mileage may vary with them. Definitely look at their own reviews and screenshots and see if they appeal to you.

My current criticisms are that the game really needs to balance out its criteria for enough dirt having been washed away to consider a segment complete--it'll either jump to finished with a substantial chunk left to clean and deprive you of that experience, or you'll spend forever walking around in circles, hitting tab, trying to find the angle that'll show you the minuscule speck of dirt that's left to clean up. 

Definitely recommend if you like the cleaning portions of House Flipper or Viscera Cleanup Detail, although it's a little flatter on the ground so far than either of those.

It's calm, perfect for those who want to chill. I love playing it with a video on the other monitor !
I'll be honest, I wasn't expecting this game to be this addictive :)

I'm torn between recommending this game and not recommending it.

If you're a person who doesn't care about getting achievements/100%'ing your games, then I think this is a great game and there's enough FREE content to keep you satisfied. There is nothing wrong with the gameplay and it's updated quite frequently with additional content, definitely worth the money for the base game.

HOWEVER, for achievement hunters this game is a nightmare. They only release new achievements for the paid content, meaning that every couple of months you get paywalled out of your perfect game and have to pay 8 dollars to go get like 10 achievements from 3-4 maps that you might not even be interested in. Going by the 2024 road map, you'll pretty much have to pay for the base game a second time (3 DLCs @ 7.99 a piece) if you want to keep it 100%.

I love this game, it's really fun and it has a dev team that consistently puts out content for the game, but the paid DLCs are overpriced and you're essentially strong-armed into buying them if you want to keep it on your perfect game list.
I hadn't seen my family in months, but then I got this game and now I don't feel like I'll ever need to see them again.
